 PROJECT: HOLIDAY SCAMS - BANKING FRAUD, IDENTITY THEFT AND HOW TO PROTECT YOURSELF
 51 minutes ago 6 min read PLEASE SHARE THIS PUBLIC DOCUMENT 
   Holiday-related fraud extends beyond fake accommodation and travel advertisements. 
 During the festive season, criminals also exploit increased financial transactions, online shopping, 
 social media activity and the public's reduced vigilance. 
 The Southern African Fraud Prevention Service (SAFPS) warned in November 2026 about fraudulent banking communications, phishing, vishing, courier impersonation and deceptive online offers. 
 These crimes can result in stolen money, compromised bank accounts and identity theft. In many cases, 
 Criminals use information collected during an initial scam to target victims again. 
 SSS urges the public to understand criminals' methods and take preventive action. 
   1. BANKING IMPERSONATION AND PHISHING: 
 Criminals contact victims while pretending to represent banks or financial institutions. 
 They may claim that suspicious transactions have occurred, an account has been compromised or a bank card requires urgent replacement. 
 Victims are manipulated into disclosing passwords, PINs, card details and one-time passwords (OTPs), or transferring money into supposedly secure accounts. 
 These scams commonly involve: 
 Phishing: Fraudulent emails, SMS messages or websites designed to steal personal and financial information. 
 Vishing: Telephone calls in which criminals impersonate trusted organisations to manipulate victims. 
 Smishing: Fraudulent SMS messages containing links to malicious websites. 
 Never disclose your banking PIN, password or OTP to someone who contacts you unexpectedly. 
 Terminate suspicious calls and contact your bank using its independently verified official number. 
   2. FAKE HOLIDAY VOUCHERS AND TIMESHARE SCAMS: 
 Criminals advertise supposedly free holidays, discounted accommodation and exclusive holiday-club memberships. 
 Victims are asked to pay upfront membership fees, administration charges or deposits in exchange for promised benefits. 
 Some schemes involve misleading contracts, hidden costs and accommodation that is unavailable when requested. 
 Before signing an agreement, verify the business, obtain all contractual terms and establish whether the advertised benefits are realistic and enforceable. 
 Never sign or pay under pressure. 
   3. FAKE INVESTMENT AND PRIZE SCAMS: 
 Fraudsters advertise investment opportunities promising unusually high returns within short periods, often with little or no risk. 
 Victims may initially receive fabricated statements or small payments to create confidence before being persuaded to transfer larger amounts. 
 Other criminals send messages claiming that the recipient has won a vehicle, cash prize or holiday package. 
 The victim is then instructed to pay an administration fee, tax or release charge before receiving the supposed prize. 
 Never pay an unknown person to release a prize you supposedly won. Independently verify investment providers and competitions before transferring money. 
   4. ONLINE DATING AND ROMANCE-RELATED FINANCIAL EXPLOITATION: 
 Criminals create fictitious dating profiles and gradually establish emotional relationships with victims. 
 Once trust has developed, they introduce financial requests involving supposed medical emergencies, travel expenses, customs charges or stranded family members. 
 Some use stolen photographs, false identities and carefully coordinated communication to maintain the deception. 
 Never send money, identity documents or banking information to someone whose identity and circumstances cannot be independently verified. 
   5. IDENTITY THEFT AND PERSONAL INFORMATION: 
 Holiday bookings, online purchases and competitions often require consumers to provide personal information. 
 Criminals exploit this process to collect identity numbers, passport details, residential addresses, banking information and other sensitive data. 
 This information can subsequently be used for: 
 Identity theft. 
 Fraudulent credit applications. 
 Bank account takeovers. 
 SIM-swap fraud. 
 Unauthorised transactions. 
 Further social engineering attacks. 
 Only provide personal information when there is a legitimate and independently verified reason to do so. 
   6. HOW TO PROTECT YOURSELF AND YOUR FAMILY: 
 SSS recommends the following preventative measures: 
 FINANCIAL SECURITY: 
 Never disclose your PIN, password or OTP. 
 Avoid transferring money into unrelated personal accounts. 
 Independently verify changes to banking details. 
 Use secure payment channels. 
 Activate available banking transaction notifications. 
 ONLINE SECURITY: 
 Avoid clicking on unsolicited links. 
 Verify websites and social media business profiles independently. 
 Use unique passwords and multifactor authentication. 
 Do not download unfamiliar applications. 
 Avoid sharing identity documents with unverified individuals. 
 HOLIDAY ARRANGEMENTS: 
 Confirm bookings directly with service providers. 
 Keep invoices, contracts and payment confirmations. 
 Check cancellation and refund conditions. 
 Be suspicious of unrealistic offers and urgent payment demands. 
 Inform trusted family members of travel arrangements without unnecessarily advertising your absence publicly. 
   7. WHAT TO DO IF YOU HAVE BEEN SCAMMED: 
 Time is critical when responding to suspected financial fraud. 
 Victims should: 
 Contact their bank immediately. Report the fraudulent transaction and ask whether the payment can be stopped, recalled or traced. 
 Secure compromised accounts. Change passwords, block affected cards and contact the mobile service provider if SIM-swap fraud is suspected. 
 Preserve evidence. Retain screenshots, advertisements, emails, WhatsApp conversations, telephone numbers, invoices and proof of payment. 
 Open a criminal case with SAPS. Provide the available evidence and obtain a case reference number. 
 Report fraudulent advertisements and accounts. Notify the relevant social media platform, booking service or retailer. 
 Notify the SAFPS. The public can report scams through its Yima platform at https://www.yima.org.za  or contact the Yima hotline on 083 123 7226. 
 Victims must also be alert to secondary recovery scams. Criminals sometimes contact people who have already lost money and promise to recover their funds in exchange for additional payments. 
 Do not delete communication with the perpetrator. It may contain important evidence. 
   8. THE BROADER CRIMINAL IMPACT: 
 Holiday fraud affects more than individual bank accounts. 
 Families may lose savings accumulated over many months, experience significant financial distress and become vulnerable to further criminal exploitation. 
 Stolen personal information can also be circulated or reused long after the original scam has taken place. 
 Reporting suspicious activities, preserving evidence and sharing verified warnings are important measures in preventing further victimisation. 
   CRIMINALS DO NOT TAKE HOLIDAYS 
 The festive season should be a time for rest, family and recreation. 
 However, criminals continue to exploit increased financial activity and public trust. 
 SSS reminds South Africans that prevention begins with awareness, independent verification 
 and responsible handling of personal and financial information. 
 If an offer appears too good to be true, investigate it before committing any money. 
 Protect your identity. Secure your accounts. Verify every transaction. Report suspicious activity. 
 Mr. Mike Bolhuis and the SSS elite Specialist Investigators encourage the public to remain vigilant 
 throughout the festive season and to share verified warnings within their communities. 
 Your financial security must remain a priority, even while you are on holiday.
